title: A general model of demand-responsive transportation services: From taxi to ridesharing to dial-a-ride

A B S T R A C T
The paper presents a general analytic framework to model transit systems that provide door-to-door service. The model includes as special cases non-shared taxi and demand responsive transportation (DRT). In the latter we include both, paratransit services such as dial-a-ride (DAR), and the form of ridesharing (shared taxi) currently being used by crowdsourced taxi companies like Lyft and Uber. The framework yields somewhat optimistic results because, among other things, it is deterministic and does not track vehicles across space. By virtue of its simplicity, however, the framework yields approximate closed form formulas for many cases of interest.

1. Introduction
Ridesharing services have emerged in many cities world-wide as new mobility solutions. In such systems, multiple travelers share the seats inside a vehicle if their itineraries are somewhat “adjacent” in a spatiotemporal sense. Properly functioning ridesharing systems are expected to increase average vehicle occupancy and reduce overall vehicle distance traveled at the city level (Fellows and Pitfield, 2000; Caulfield, 2009; Masoud and Jayakrishnan, 2017), and at the same time be attractive to individual travelers by reducing their “share” of the travel cost (Chan and Shaheen, 2012; Furuhata et al., 2013). Associated benefits also include fuel savings (Jacobson and King, 2009) and reduction in GHG emissions (Yu et al., 2017).

To understand why this is significant, consider the fundamental inefficiency of traditional private car travel: most vehicles operate with only one or two occupants, wasting the vast majority of their available seating capacity. Ridesharing addresses this by acting as a spatial and temporal matching engine. When two passengers have origins and destinations that are close to each other in both space and time, they can share a single vehicle. This "adjacency" is the key constraint. If the detour required to pick up a second passenger is too long or too circuitous, the system will not match them, preserving the efficiency of the trip. By maximizing the number of passengers per vehicle, these systems theoretically reduce the total number of cars needed on the road, leading to the cited benefits of lower fuel consumption and reduced greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.

In addition to conventional door-to-door mobility services via non-shared taxi and dial-a-ride (DAR), newer mobility services, such as those by Uber and Lyft in the U.S., and DidiChuxing in China, cover a range of ride-sharing alternatives such as shared taxi and carpooling. All these systems differ in terms of key characteristics such as typical vehicle occupancy, expected waiting time, expected in-vehicle riding time, as well passenger-vehicle matching rules. For example, conventional taxi features single occupancy rides served by a relatively large fleet of vehicles, such that passengers experience relatively low waiting time. Dial-a-ride systems, at the other extreme, typically run a small number of vehicles that are shared by many passengers—who are expected to spend more time waiting for pickup and in the vehicles. The current “shared taxi” services by Uber/Lyft (e.g., Uber Pool) are qualitatively in between conventional taxis and DAR; i.e., passengers experience relatively short waits, share the vehicle with a small number of peers, and may endure significant detours before being dropped off. In some other systems, riders are even allowed to transfer between multiple vehicles along their trips

Planning and operating ride-sharing services, particularly in a dynamic setting, is usually challenging. One school of thought handles this problem through discrete optimization and/or detailed simulations (e.g., Luo and Schonfeld, 2007; Hosni et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2018). Agatz et al. (2012) gives a detailed review of optimization schemes for the dynamic ride matching problem. Another example in this school of thought is Agatz et al. (2011), which develops, both, a weighted bipartite matching model to pair drivers and riders dynamically, and a simulation study that tracked actual travel data from the Atlanta metropolitan area. More recently, the potential of using self-driving vehicles for dynamic ridesharing in the City of Austin, Texas, has been examined through agent-based simulations (Fagnant and Kockelman, 2018). These detailed simulation and optimization approaches are quite powerful, but they require much input data, which may not always be reliable, and the numerical solutions they produce may hide general insights that could be useful for planning.

In efforts to obtain designs that are more general and insightful, albeit less precise, compact analytical models have been developed that require fewer and less detailed inputs. This can be done, for example, by treating the ridesharing systems as distributed open queuing networks similar to those in the manufacturing literature (e.g., Bitran and Dasu, 1992), or as networks of economic input/output production systems (Yang and Yang, 2011). This approach allows the modeler to build approximate mathematical formulas that capture a system's steady-state performance, even if the system is very large and complex. Even for entire cities, the key system trade-offs can be expressed on the basis of very few data items, in terms of just a few decision variables such as the fleet size and a target for average vehicle occupancy. Solutions to these simpler models can often be obtained analytically, and the resulting insights can be ideal for high-level decision-making. For a more extended discussion of this topic see Daganzo et al. (2012).

Analytical models of the type just discussed have been used in the design and operations of non-shared taxi systems based on street hailing (e.g., Yang and Yang, 2011) and e-hailing (e.g., Zha et al., 2018), dial-a-ride systems (Daganzo 1977; Daganzo et al., 1977), dial-a-ride systems with transfers (Daganzo 1984), and flexible-route paratransit systems (Nourbakhsh and Ouyang, 2012). Meanwhile, parallel efforts have also been made to study optimal fleet configuration and service design of traditional fixed-route transit (Daganzo, 2010; Jara-Diaz et al., 2017) and flexible-route transit (Kim and Schonfeld, 2012; Kim et al., 2018), and integration of different systems to provide multimodal services (Kim and Schonfeld, 2014; Chen and Nie 2017). All these efforts, however, treat ride-sharing systems individually, with ad-hoc approaches that are different for each system.

To the authors' knowledge, the literature still lacks an overarching model that can encompass a large family of systems, so they can be compared both generically and generally. Such a general model would also allow answering (at least approximately) some of the questions faced by mobility service providers as they plan to enter a new market; e.g.: $^{1}$ What type of services shall we offer? What should be the service quality? How many resources (e.g., number of vehicles and drivers) shall we acquire? How should we manage these resources so as to meet the level of service target while minimizing our cost? As a small first step toward filling these gaps, this paper presents a general analytic framework that can be used to model steady-state performance of various demand-responsive transit systems.

The proposed general model will encompass non-shared taxi, dial-a-ride, and ridesharing (shared taxi) as special cases $^{2}$ . Using existing formulas for conventional transit and the private automobile, the new model will allow us to compare the existing urban transportation modes in scenarios involving different city types and levels of demand. To do this, the remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 formulates the general model. Sections 3–5

develop the special cases for: (i) non-shared taxis, (ii) dial-a-ride, and (iii) two types of crowd-sourced ride-sharing services. Then, Section 6 verifies the analytical formulas with simulations, and Section 7 presents some conclusions.

To truly understand the implications of Equation (9), let's break down its three distinct terms, as each represents a different operational cost or resource requirement within the fleet.

1.  **The Base Fleet ($n$):** The first term, $n$, represents the core number of vehicles needed to handle the steady-state demand. This is the fundamental capacity of the system.
2.  **The Buffer for Variability ($k \pi n ^ {- 1 / 2}$):** The second term is particularly interesting. It scales with $n^{-1/2}$, meaning it grows with the square root of the fleet size. This term acts as a statistical buffer. In stochastic systems, as the number of independent events (like passenger requests) increases, the relative variability decreases, but the absolute number of "extra" vehicles needed to maintain a high service level (determined by the parameter $k$) still increases. Think of it like a safety stock in a warehouse: even if your average daily sales are predictable, you still need extra inventory to cover unexpected spikes. Here, $k$ controls how conservative we are; a higher $k$ means we are willing to keep more idle vehicles to ensure that we almost never run out of cars when a passenger calls.
3.  **The Assignment Overhead ($k \pi$):** The final term, $k \pi$, is a constant offset related to the specific algorithmic constraints and the probability of assignment success. It represents a fixed overhead cost associated with the matching process itself, independent of the scale of the fleet $n$.

This formula tells us that while the fleet size grows linearly with demand ($n$), the efficiency gains from scale mean that the *proportion* of vehicles needed for safety buffers decreases as the system gets larger. This is a classic result in queueing theory and operations research: larger systems are more stable relative to their size.

We are trying to determine how many private cars would be needed to serve the same demand as the public transport systems we've been discussing. To do this, we rely on **Little's Law** (or Little's Formula), a fundamental principle in queueing theory and operations management. The law states that the average number of items in a system ($L$) is equal to the arrival rate ($\lambda$) multiplied by the average time an item spends in the system ($W$). In our context:
*   $L$ is the number of cars in circulation.
*   $\lambda$ is the rate at which trips are requested (demand).
*   $W$ is the average duration of a trip.

The text tells us the average trip length is $(2/3)R^{1/2}$. If we assume vehicles travel at a constant speed $v$, the time for a trip is simply distance divided by speed: $W = \frac{(2/3)R^{1/2}}{v}$. Plugging this into Little's Law ($L = \lambda \cdot W$), we get:
$$ L = \lambda \cdot \frac{(2/3)R^{1/2}}{v} = \frac{2}{3} \lambda R^{3/2} v^{-1} $$
The text then notes that under the specific parameters of this study, this value simplifies to approximately 66 cars. This single dot on the graph represents the "private car benchmark." It answers the question: "If everyone drove their own car, how many cars would be on the road at any given moment?"

Of course, this dot is somewhat optimistic as it does not consider the lost time usually associated with cruising for parking at the destination, or the costs for parking during the day and garaging the vehicle at night.

It is vital to recognize the limitations of this benchmark. The calculation of 66 cars assumes a perfect world where a car is only "in use" while moving from point A to point B. In reality, a significant portion of a car's life is spent searching for parking, sitting in a parking lot, or stored in a garage. By ignoring these "dead times," the private car option appears more efficient than it truly is. If we were to account for the hours spent cruising for parking or the infrastructure costs of garaging, the effective "fleet size" required to support private car travel would be significantly higher. This makes the private car dot a lower bound—a best-case scenario for private ownership.

7. Concluding remarks
The results in this note are just a beginning. Although the provided method is reasonably accurate, especially for large systems with heavy demand, it is not perfectly realistic. The main simplification is that the assignment algorithms used by service providers are likely to be much more complicated than what we studied. For example, the analysis assumes that passenger assignments in the taxi cases are instantaneous, but in reality there is a delay. Furthermore, service providers may consider the alignment of destinations in making assignment decisions, and not just origins.

is crucial to recognize the gap between this theoretical model and the messy reality of urban transportation. Real-world dispatching algorithms are not just looking for the *nearest* car; they are optimizing for complex future states. They might assign a car that is slightly further away because that car is heading in the same direction as the passenger's destination, thereby reducing the empty miles the car will drive after dropping the passenger off. By ignoring destination alignment and assuming instantaneous matching, our model provides a lower bound on efficiency—a best-case scenario that real systems strive to approach but rarely achieve perfectly.

Despite all these shortcomings, however, the evidence seems to suggest that the analytical model can be used by taxi companies and government agencies to systematically explore operating and pricing strategies. They could also be used by cities to begin to understand how taxi companies might respond to different forms of regulation.
Even an imperfect model is invaluable if it reveals the *direction* and *magnitude* of effects, such as how a 10% increase in fleet size impacts average wait times.

Further research can be conducted in many directions. First, this paper examines one type of mobility service at a time, while in the real world there are typically multiple technologies operating at the same time. It is of equal or even more importance to decide how multiple systems can work together to best serve a pool of travel demand; and how to make this happen with smart regulations. Another topic for future research is to determine the conditions under which coordination and joint service across multiple services could be useful (e.g., in big cities)—or not. Third, in each of our dispatching strategies, we only assign the nearest suitable vehicle to a passenger along the shortest path. Other assignment and routing schemes (e.g., based on dynamic programming and/or dynamic bipartite matching) could potentially improve system performance; e.g., see Lei et al. (2019). Future research could probably explore the extent to which such improvements can be achieved, and how such dynamic assignment schemes can be implemented in a real-time setting. Finally, the model could be extended so as to address more complicated request arrival processes; e.g., those spatiotemporally heterogeneous, and those demanding multiple seats in one request.
